2.3.14.3 Non-installation of capacitors

The power load demand in the State is being met with the availability of
power from self generation share in central sector power projects and power
purchased from the Northern Grid. The State mostly depends upon the
drawal of power from Northern Grid and due to excessive drawal of reactive
power the system voltage is substantially low. Reactive power is a concept to
describe the background energy movement in an alternating current system
arising from production of electric and magnetic fields. These fields store
energy which changes through each AC cycle. Devices which store energy
by virtue of electric fields are said to generate reactive power such as, electric
motors, welding sets, etc. The dissipation of power due to such devices
reduces power factor (ratio of real power to apparent power) and has to be
made up by way of devices which store energy by virtue of magnetic field
and are said to absorb reactive power such as capacitors. Consumers with a
power factor below 96 per cent are assessed with reactive power measured in
Kilo Volt Ampere Reactive (KVAR) charge. In order to improve the power
factor and the system voltage profile and also to reduce the drawal of reactive
current from the Northern Grid, all State Electricity Boards were asked to
install shunt capacitors in their respective networks.

The power utility was required to devise different modules of training for

2.3.21 Conclusion

The State had not been able to take full advantage of the assistance given by
the Government of India as it had not been able to implement the projects in
a time bound manner. Plan funds to the extent of 49 per cent only were
utilized by the Department during the period 2007-08 to 2011-12. A State
Electricity Plan and State Electricity Policy, as provided in the Jammu and
Kashmir Electricity Act, 2010, to give shape to the future requirements in the
Transmission Sector and to provide a roadmap for development of Power
system in the State, had not been formulated despite lapse of about two years.
The Department had failed to achieve the planned targets during 2007-12 and
almost all the Grid sub-station and Transmission line projects started under
Prime Minister’s Reconstruction Plan (PMRP) had witnessed a time overrun.
Some of the completed projects could not be operationalised due to
incompletion of other related works with the result the infrastructure created
was lying idle. The projects had suffered due to unplanned project
formulations, execution of projects on adhoc basis and execution of projects
without availability of essential pre-planning stage components like land,
Right of Way, well formulated structural designs, site conditions, sound bid
evaluation, etc. The transmission losses exceeded the Central Electricity
Authority (CEA) norm of four per cent and ranged between 5.07 and 8.14
per cent during the period 2008-09 to 2011-12. In-efficient Grid
management had led to payment of Unscheduled Interchage (UD) charges to
the Northern Regional Electricity Board (NREB). The Department failed to
install Power Factor (PF) correction capacitor banks resulted in payment of &
220.65 crore on account of ‘Reactive Energy’ charges during the period
2002-03 to 2011-12. Against requirement of = 160.65 crore for maintenance
of transmission assets, € 36.33 crore was provided during the period 2007-08
to 2011-12 indicating ignorance of the Department in the maintenance of the
assets. The Department did not setup Disaster Management system in all the
power utilities in the State due to paucity of funds.

241 Introduction

Government of India (GOI) enacted (August 1996)' the Building and Other
Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act,
1996 (BOCW Act) for constitution of a Welfare Board in each State to undertake
social security schemes”. The GOI also enacted (August 1996)? the Building and
Other Construction Workers Welfare Cess Act, 1996 (Cess Act). Section 14 of the
Cess Act stipulates that rule making power under the Act vests only with the GOI.
The GOI framed (March 1998) the Building and other Construction Workers Welfare
Cess Rules, 1998 (Cess Rules). To augment the resources of the Board, Section 3 of
the Cess Act as amended in September 1996 provided for levy and collection of
labour welfare cess at a uniform rate of one percent of the cost of construction
incurred by the employer. For the safety, health and welfare of the workers, the State
Government in pursuance of sections 40 and 62 of the BOCW Act also framed
(uly 2006) the Jammu and Kashmir Building and Other Construction Workers
(Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Rules, 2006 (J&KBOCW
Rules) as amended in November 2012. The State Government constituted (July 2007)
the Jammu and Kashmir Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board
(Board) to carry out welfare schemes for construction workers. The provisions of
BOCW Act are applicable to every establishment which employs, or had employed on
any day of the preceding 12 months, 10 or more workers in any building or other
construction works. All such establishments engaged in construction activity are
liable to pay cess under the Cess Act except construction activity by an employer in
relation to his residence costing less than हैं 10 lakh (excluding the cost of land).

2.4.2 Organisational set-up

To oversee the implementation of the BOCW and Cess Acts, the State Government
had appointed (January 2007) the Labour Commissioner of the State as Chief
Inspector and Appellate Authority, two Deputy Labour Commissioners as Assessing
Officers (one each for Kashmir and Jammu province), 22 Assistant Labour
Commissioners as Registering Officers/ Cess Collectors and 24 Labour Officers as
Inspectors for the whole State within their respective jurisdiction.

The Board is headed by the Hon’ble Minister of Labour and Employment as
Chairman. The other members of the Board are Welfare Commissioner (Hgr.),
Ministry of Labour and Employment, GOI and 15 representatives, five each from the
State Government, employers and workers. The Secretary of the Board was an officer
of State Government of the rank of Deputy Secretary (October 2012).

2.4.5.1 Delay in formation of Jammu and Kashmir Building and Other

Construction Workers Welfare Board

It was noticed that the implementation of the BOCW Act, 1996 was not ensured
expeditiously by the State Government as the Board was constituted (July 2007) after
a delay of 11 years from the date of enactment of BOCW Act and reconstituted in
December 2010. The Board actually started collecting the cess under the Act from
November 2008 and started incurring expenditure only from February 2011. The
delay in constitution and operation of the Board resulted in non-enforcement of
provisions of the Act for the social security and other welfare measures of workers
besides loss of cess to the Board. During test-check of records, Audit noticed non-
recovery of cess of हैं 41.69 lakh from the bills of the contractors by two Executive
Engineers’.

Schedule for holding meetings by the Board was not prescribed in J&K BOCW Rules,
2006 as required under Section 20 of BOCW (RECS) Act, 1996. The Supreme Court
had also directed (February 2012) that the Board shall meet once in two months. The
rules amended in November 2012, however, provide that the Board shall ordinarily
meet once in two months. It was, however, noticed that the Board had met thrice
(February 2011, July 2011 and February 2012) since its establishment (July 2007)
which resulted in shortfall in conducting meetings and taking policy decisions for the
welfare of the construction workers.

2.4.9 Internal Control System and Monitoring mechanism

2.4.9.1 Internal Audit and Internal Control Systems

Internal Audit and Internal Control Systems are important mechanisms for ensuring
the smooth working of an organisation. While effective Internal Control Mechanism
helps in exercising check on various activities of the organisation, Internal Audit acts
as an effective tool in exercising check on expenditure. It also ensures that various
systems are functioning properly.

Audit noticed the following deficiencies in the internal control system;

e The Cash Book in the CEO/ Secretary Office had been maintained on the basis of
bank scrolls. However, with effect from February 2011, the cheques of cess
amount were entered in the Cheque Receipt Register instead of Cash Book. The
records indicating details of cheques received, credit afforded on these cheques by
the bank to the account of the Board and cheques dishonoured were not
maintained by the Board.

e  Test-check of records of six ALCs revealed that the Cash Books were not closed
daily/ monthly by three ALCs (Baramulla, Bandipora and Srinagar) and three
ALCs (Poonch, Samba and Jammu) had not maintained Cash Book with the result
that genuineness of balances reflected in the bank statement could not be
reconciled.

The Secretary/ CEO stated (August 2012) that the necessary guidance of Audit has
been noted.

© The Board had not introduced any Internal Audit in order to ensure effective
control in exercising checks on various activities of the Board including its
finances. In reply to an audit query, the Secretary/ CEO of the Board stated
(July 2012) that the instructions had been noted.

2.4.9.2 Non-preparation of Annual report

Section 26 of the BOCW Act, 1996 envisages that the Board shall prepare, in such
form and at such time of each financial year as may be prescribed, its annual report,
giving a full account of its activities during the previous financial year and submit a
copy thereof to the State Government and Central Government. It was noticed in audit
that the Board had not prepared the requisite annual reports for the financial years
2010-11 and 2011-12.

2.4.10 Monitoring mechanism

The Board had empowered (July 2011) the CEO/ Secretary to take up the process of
implementation of the scheme by constituting committees at district level for
monitoring the implementation of the Act in an effective manner, Such committees
were to meet at regular intervals to give necessary feedback to the Board for removal
of the difficulties in smooth implementation of the scheme. Out of 22 monitoring
committees, only four committees (Reasi, Samba, Ganderbal and Kargil) had
furnished feedback to the Board. Thus, the very purpose of constitution of district
level committees for the better implementation of the Act could not be achieved. The
Secretary stated (August 2012) that the matter had been taken up with all the District
Commissioners and only some of them had shown keen interest in implementing the
Act. Audit further noticed that no meetings were conducted by the ALCs with the
district heads, etc. with regard to the implementation of the Act as no such reports
were on record with the ALCs.

2411 Conclusion

The State Government started implementation of the BOCW and Cess Acts after a
delay of more than 11 years from their enactments. The J&K Building and Other
Construction Workers Welfare Board after its constitution in March 2007 did not take
any initiatives to formulate the modalities for implementing the welfare schemes till
February 2011. The State Advisory Committee was not constituted even after more
than 16 years of enactment of the Act to advice the Board on such matters arising out
of the administration of the Act, as may be referred to it. The crucial aspects of
identification of beneficiaries and registration of establishments and implementation
of welfare schemes for workers were not given due priority. As a result, huge funds to
the extent of हैं 100.62 crore remained unutilised with the Board as of March 2012.
Expenditure to the tune of = 73.22 lakh had been incurred in excess of the permissible
limit during 2010-12 on establishment and other expenditure in contravention of the
Act. The monitoring mechanism was weak and internal audit and internal control
system had also not been instituted by the Board.

2.5. Fraudulent drawals

Non-observance of prescribed checks by the Principal, Government Girls
Higher Secondary School and Treasury Officer, Bhaderwah facilitated
fraudulent drawals of % 3.26 lakh.

Rule 2.27 of the Jammu and Kashmir Financial Code provide that the disbursing
officer should enter all bills drawn from the Treasury for departmental expenditure in
a register and get all drawals verified with the registers maintained at the Treasury
once in a month. Further, the rules stipulate that all monetary transactions should be
entered in the cash book as soon as they occur and should be attested by the Head of
the office in token of check.

The procedure for drawal of money from Treasury involves the following steps:

a. preparation and submission of the bills duly attested by the Drawing and
Disbursing Officer (DDO) to the Treasury;

b transferring of money by the Treasury into the official account of the DDO
and recording the entry of payment by the Treasury Officer in treasury records viz.,
Register in Form-3 (Madhwar);

०. recording of the entries of drawal of money by the DDO in his drawal register
and cash book and

व्‌. periodical reconciliation of the cash book balances with the drawal register
and the Bank account statement by the DDO. For this purpose, the DDO is to obtain
from the Treasury Officer by the 15" of every month, a list of bills drawn during the
previous month and trace them in the cash book.

Audit check (December 2010) of records of the Principal, Government Girls Higher
Secondary School, Bhaderwah (DDO) by way of verification of transactions recorded
in the drawal register with the Bank Account statement of the DDO and the records of
Treasury Bhaderwah revealed that three drawals' amounting to हैं 2.46 lakh were
drawn (January 2009 and February 2010) from the Treasury and had not been
recorded in drawal register and cash book of the DDO. These drawals were made on
the basis of fictitious claims of General Provident Fund (GPF) advance (% 1.30 lakh)
of two officials and pay arrears of the staff (¥ 1.16 lakh) from the Treasury. The
entries thereof were not recorded in the drawal register, cash book and GPF advance
register of the office or the personal records of the employees. The amounts after
transfer by the treasury to the official account of the DDO were subsequently credited
to the bank accounts of a fake official (January 2009) and senior assistant of the office
(February 2010) respectively on the basis of authority letters issued by the DDO. A
check of treasury records (Madhwar) and the drawal register revealed that the
Treasury Officer without verifying the drawals made by the DDO during January
2009 and February 2010 from his records had recorded wrong certificates of
verification of drawals on the drawal register.

The matter was pointed out (December 2010) in Audit to the Principal, Government

placed (December 2011) under suspension and the ex-Principal had been charge
sheeted (December 2011) and that the amount of & 3.26 lakh had been remitted into
the Treasury/paid to the concerned officials by the senior assistant.

Thus, non-observance of prescribed checks by the Principal, Government Girls
Higher Secondary School and Treasury Officer, Bhaderwah facilitated fraudulent
drawals of = 3.26 lakh by the DDO. The risk of drawal of GPF advances on fake bills
may be minimised by establishing a system of intimating to the concerned employee

2.21.7 Planning

Proper planning is essential for success of the programme. The District Industries
Centres (DICs) were required to conduct and update the industrial survey of the
districts for assessing the industrial potential including availability of human
resources and raw material, marketing avenues and other factors for preparation of
Perspective Plan and Annual Plans at periodical intervals. Audit scrutiny revealed
that no such survey was conducted by the DICs of the Department. The Director,
Industries and Commerce, Jammu stated (July 2012) that the General Managers of
respective DICs would be asked to conduct such surveys. The Joint Director
Development, Directorate of Industries and Commerce, Kashmir, however, stated
(August 2012) that such surveys were conducted while identifying land for industrial
estates through field agencies. The Commissioner/Secretary reported (December
2012) that fresh potential survey had been conducted and communicated to the
Government of India by the District Industries Centres of the Kashmir valley. The
reply should be viewed in light of the fact that General Managers of three test-
checked DICs (Srinagar, Baramulla and Anantnag) had stated that no such survey
was conducted in the districts.

To accelerate industrial development of the State and boost investor-confidence, the
Government of India sanctioned special package of incentives in June 2002. To
supplement this, the State Government had also sanctioned (January 2004) its own
package of incentives under the State Industrial Policy 2004. One of the objectives
of State Industrial Policy 2004 was to generate 90 per cent employment in the
industrial units. The Department was not monitoring whether the industrial units set
up under the Central/State Government’ s industrial promotion policies and provided
with fiscal incentives and subsidies were indeed meeting the objective of
employment generation as laid down in the State Industrial Policy 2004. The
employment generated data was accepted as claimed by the industrial units without
any mechanism for verification being in place. There is no mechanism in place to
monitor the turnover, value of output, profitability, extent and quality of
employment generation, actual new investment brought in and extent of value
addition in the manufacturing by the units so as to see whether these are
commensurate with the burden of tax concessions and subsidies on the public
exchequer besides, facilitating balanced geographically well-dispersed growth as
evident from the succeeding paragraphs

2.21.21.1 Integrated Handloom Development Scheme

To facilitate the sustainable development of handloom weavers located in or outside
identified clusters into a cohesive, self-managing and competitive socio-economic
unit, the Government of India had launched a Centrally sponsored scheme ‘Integrated
Handloom Development Scheme (IHDS)’ to be implemented during the 117 Five
Year Plan period (2007-12). Under this scheme, 10 cluster projects (estimated cost:
% 5.91 crore) and 17 Group Approach Projects (estimated cost: % 1.21 crore) were
sanctioned by the GOI during 2007-08 and 2009-11 respectively. For the cluster
projects of the scheme, the guidelines envisage formation of consortium involving
stake holders from the Self Help Groups (SHGs), co-operative societies, master
weavers, private entrepreneurs, NGOs for interaction with the weavers, etc.

To ensure regular availability of yarn of requisite count and to avoid delay in
production process, one time assistance of & three lakh per cluster was to be provided
as a corpus fund to National Handloom Development Corporation (NHDC) to ensure
supply of yarn to the weavers against payment through yarn depots at the cluster.
Further, to provide facilities of pre-loom and post-loom operations, quality control
laboratory, common work shed, water treatment and effluent treatment plants to
weavers, common facility centre was to be set up in each cluster.

It was noticed that consortium was formed from weavers of the area only and did not
involve SHGs, private entrepreneurs, cooperative societies and NGOs. The Assistant
Director, Handlooms Kathua stated (July 2012) that necessary steps would be taken to
include SHGs, NGOs, private entrepreneurs, etc. in the consortium.

Further, no yarn depot was set up and no corpus fund was maintained in any of the
test-checked clusters as yarn was supplied to weavers free of cost. The yarn supplied
was also utilized for imparting training and for making samples which defeated the
purpose of creation of corpus fund.

are proposed, extent of manual mining or mining by use of machinery and mechanical
devices, details of scheme of restoration of the area by afforestation, land reclamation
and such other measures as directed by the Government, annual programme and plan
for excavation during five years. The mining operations are required to be carried out
in accordance with the duly approved mining plan. Test-check of records showed that

2.21.28 Illegal mining

The Environment Protection Act, 1986 provides that no mining should be carried out
in wildlife reserve area. The Hon’ble Supreme Court of India notified (December
2006) areas falling within 10 kilometers of the boundary of National Park and
Wildlife Sanctuaries as eco-sensitive zones and extraction of minerals in such areas
was prohibited. The Department however, did not adhere to the provisions of the Act
and the directions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and instead granted mining lease to
lessees for extraction of Gypsum within and in the vicinity of Kazinag National Park
and Limber-Lachipora Wildlife Sanctuary despite reservations raised (April/October
2010) by the Ministry of Environment and Forests (Wildlife Division), Government
of India and Commissioner/Secretary to the State Government, Forest Department. It

areas led to illegal mining which indicated casual approach of the Department towards

Mining, Kashmir stated (March 2012) that notification of the Hon’ble Supreme Court

The terms and conditions of the State Pollution Control Board (SPCB) envisage

of one year, thereby violating norms of Pollution Control Board. The consent of
operation for five lessees operating in mining sites at Batote, Galija, Jathi Assar,
Buniyar and Salamabad Uri had not been got renewed by these lessees despite lapse
of three to four years from the dates of lapse of previous consents (March 2012). The
SPCB had not taken any action against these lessees for violation of Water
(Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and Air (Prevention and Control of
Pollution) Act, 1981, as a result, these lessees continued to extract Gypsum
unauthorisedly, This indicated lack of concern of the Department over the
environmental issues. The SPCB stated (March 2012) that notices are being issued to
the defaulters and action is being taken towards issuing closure notices in respect of
defaulter units.

2.21.33 Monitoring and Evaluation

Monitoring and evaluation is an effective tool to ascertain the effect and impact of the
programmes undertaken for implementation by the Department. For effective and
efficient implementation of the State Industrial Policy 2004 regular interactions
between the State Government at the highest level and the industry were to be held for
discussion of major issues relating to the industry. For this purpose, an Advisory
Committee for Industries with the Hon’ble Chief Minister as the Chairman, Hon’ble
Minister for Industries and Commerce, all Principal Secretaries in charge of the
Economic Departments, representatives of Chambers of Commerce and Industries and
Federations of Industries of the State and senior officials of the Ministry of
Commerce and Industry, GOI was to be set up and the committee had to meet once in
every three months. It was, however, seen in audit that the Advisory Committee was
set up during the year 2009-10 after about five years of sanction of the State Industrial
Policy 2004 and its first meeting was held in February 2012. As a result, the objective
of setting up of the Committee to monitor implementation of the State Industrial
Policy 2004 could not be achieved. Audit further observed that monitoring of training
centres had not been conducted at district level. Besides, evaluation of the programme
had never been conducted. As a result, the impact of the programme could not be
ascertained. The Joint Director, Handicraft, Jammu stated (April 2012) that evaluation
of the programme was conducted on monthly and quarterly basis. The reports of
evaluation of the programme conducted, if any, were however not shown to audit.

the Department were not adhered to as discussed below:

¢ The Administrative Department as well as the Directors had not maintained a

2.21.35 Conclusion

The employment generation and value addition by the industrial units getting fiscal
concessions and subsidies from Central and State Governments was not
commensurate with the burden of exchequer. These beneficiary units were also not
geographically well-dispersed, concentrated around railheads closer to neighbouring
States. There were cases of diversion/misutilisation of funds towards payment of
salaries/wages, etc. Overpayments/irregular payments to entrepreneurs were noticed
due to non-observance of guidelines/instructions governing packages of incentives.
The performance of various Central Schemes in Handicraft and Handloom sector was
poor. There was lack of adequate monitoring of training centres. The Department had
no mechanism in place to check the quantities of minerals extracted and lifted by the
lessees from the mineral sites.

3.9 Response of the Departments/Government towards audit

periodical inspection of the Government Departments to test check the transactions

in the rules. These inspections are followed up with Inspection Reports (IRs)
incorporating irregularities detected during the inspection and not settled on the spot,
which were issued to the heads of the offices with copies to the next higher authorities
for taking prompt corrective action. The Heads of offices/Government are required to
comply promptly with the observations contained in the IRs, rectify the defects and
omissions and report compliance through initial reply to the PAG’s office within one
month from the date of receipt of the IRs. Serious financial irregularities are reported to
the heads of the Departments and the Government.

REVENUE SECTOR : AUDIT FINDINGS
A. Performance Audit

FINANCE DEPARTMENT

Taxes on Services

Highlights

4.1.1

The revenue collection trends have been buoyant, steadily increasing from
हूँ 266.83 crore in 2007-08 to = 697.69 crore in 2011-12. However, the
number of registered dealers has not shown corresponding increase
suggesting higher revenue yield from a smaller group of dealers.
(Paragraph: 4.1.7)

The Department had not conducted any survey to identify unregistered
service providers and get them registered. Audit noticed evasion of
service tax of = 7.66 crore due to non-registration of dealers engaged in
insurance business with the Department.
(Paragraph: 4.1.9)
The consumption account of material purchased by 17 dealers on
concessional rates was not verified at the time of their assessment. On
cross verification, the concealment of purchases of % 1.20 crore with tax
liability of = 31.70 lakh was detected.
(Paragraph: 4.1.10)

Short deduction of service tax of = 78 lakh by 37 DDOs was noticed by
Audit.

(Paragraph: 4.1.11)

The penalty amounting to हैं 2.62 crore against 119 DDOs for their failures
by way of short deduction, delayed credit of tax and non-submission of
contract agreements was not imposed.

(Paragraphs: 4.1.11, 4.1.12 and 4.1.13)
Introduction.

Service tax is levied on the taxable services by the Union Government under Chapter-
V of the Finance Act, 1994. This Chapter extends to whole of India except the State
of Jammu and Kashmir. However, the taxation of services in the State began when the
Government in exercise of the powers conferred under Section 4 of the Jammu &
Kashmir General Sales Tax Act, 1962 (Referred to as Act) brought photo finishing
service under taxation with effect from March 1997 followed by four more services
including works contract from July 1997. Further, 14 services were brought under
taxation during the period from September 2003 to March 2011. The tax was levied

175


Audit Report on Social, General, Revenue and Economic Sectors (Non-PSUs) for the year ended 31 March 2012

and collected by the State and credited to the Consolidated Fund of the State. As at
the end of March 2012, a total 20 services’ were taxable in the State.

4.1.2 Organisational set up

The Commissioner, Commercial Taxes J&K (CCT) is responsible for the overall
control and superintendence of taxes on services in the State, who is under the
administrative control of State Finance Department. The Commissioner is assisted by
three Additional Commissioners of Commercial Taxes and 13 Deputy Commissioners
of Commercial taxes. There are 52 commercial taxes assessment circles (Jammu: 25;
Kashmir: 27) each headed by one Commercial Taxes Officer (CTO) in the State. Of
these, two Circles (‘H’ Srinagar and ‘O’ Jammu) deal exclusively with assessment of
service tax of contractors engaged in providing of services in the shape of execution
of works contracts.

4.1.3 Scope of Audit

Test-check of assessment records of ten assessment circles (Jammu: Six and Kashmir:

Four) and two Additional Commissioners (Admn) Commercial Taxes was conducted

during the period from July 2011 to April 2012. The period covered under audit was

4.1.8 Revenue potential of the Tax on Services under the State Law vis-a-vis
foregone share of the State in the Central Service Tax

Service Tax is the only Central tax that is presently not applicable to the State of
Jammu & Kashmir because, unlike other States, Jammu and Kashmir levies tax on
services under its own law, viz., the Jammu and Kashmir General Sales Tax (GST)
Act, 1962. Hence, the State gets a share in all Central taxes/duties except in the total

1.551 per cent of the Service tax collection by the Central Government during

regarding likely (Central) Service Tax collection during 2010-15, the 1.551 per cent
share foregone by the State of Jammu and Kashmir works out to % 8363.38 crore.
During 2010-11, the State’s foregone share in Central Service Tax was about हैं 1100
crore whereas the total collection by the State on ‘Services’ under the J&K GST Act

paid out of the State Budget for financing various public works and infrastructure
development projects). The State tax on services of ‘works contracts’ includes a

revenue gain to the State exchequer from the tax on pure services collected from non-
Government tax payers under the State law is and likely to remain significantly lower
than the share in the Central Service Tax being foregone by the State.

The Finance Department informed (January 2013) that the Government would

4.1.9 Inadequate efforts to broaden the tax base

tax under the Act, carry on business as a dealer unless he has been registered in

providers (dealers) and ensuring payment of service tax, the Department has relied
mainly on voluntary compliance. The growth of revenue is directly linked with the
growth of the base of service providers. Audit observed that the Department had not
conducted any survey to identify unregistered service providers and get them
registered.

As per Section 6 (i) of the Jammu and Kashmir GST Act if any person carries on
business as a dealer in contravention of the Act, the appropriate Authority is required

exceeding rupees five thousand for the default.

4.1.10 Non-verification of consumption account of material

The Assessing Authorities allow contractors rendering services in the shape of works
contracts to import specific building material/plant and machinery from outside the
State on concessional rates against ‘C’ forms on the recommendations of the works
executing Agencies/Department. The Assessing Authorities while assessing these
contractors, were required to obtain consumption accounts of these goods and ensure
that material imported against ‘C’ forms on concessional rates had been
consumed/utilised on the works for which such material was allowed to be imported.

Test-check of records of three circles* revealed that 17 dealers had been allowed by
the Assessing Authorities to purchase building material and plant and machinery
worth हैं 20.51 crore during the period from 2003-04 to 2008-09 against ‘C’ forms on
concessional rates of tax. However, at the time of assessments of these dealers made
during 2007-08 to 2010-11, the Assessing Authorities did not obtain the consumption
account of such material utilised by the contractors for the works. As a result the
genuineness of concession of tax allowed to the contractors could not be ascertained.

On this being pointed out by audit, the Assessing Authority circle ‘O’ Jammu stated

4.1.15 Ineffective monitoring of returns

Section 7 of the J&K GST Act, 1962 provides that every dealer liable to pay tax shall

due failing which he shall be liable to a penalty at the rate of two per cent per
month of the tax payable as reduced by the amount of the tax paid during the
period of default or $1000, whichever is higher.

Test-check of records of four Circles” revealed that 21 dealers had filed the returns
beyond the prescribed time and the delay ranged between I(one) and 55 months.
While finalising the assessment (2009-10 to 2011-12), the AAs had not levied penalty

4.2 Assessment and collection of water usage charges

As a part of its commitments to reduce fiscal deficit under the fiscal
responsibility legislation, the Government expects all departments to recover at
least 50 per cent of the ‘service charges’ from the users after accounting for
operations and maintenance expenses, as recommended by the 13th Finance
Commission. An Audit Review of the performance of water usage charges
indicated that the gap between Revenue receipts and Revenue expenditure on

was governed under the provisions of Jammu and Kashmir Water Supply Act,

Management) Act 2010. The mechanism for fixation of targets and framing of
Budget estimates on realistic basis did not exist in the Department. Audit also
noticed delays in remittance of revenue into the Government account, shortfall in
revenue realization ranging between 40 and 55 per cent.

4.2.8.3 Non-issue of water charge bills

According to Rule 10 of J&K Water Resources (Regulation and Management) Rules

registered consumers in the state for ensuring credibility and transparency though
taken up by the Department had not been completed fully as a result of which the
department was not in a position to issue computerized water usage bills to all the
consumers of the State. Audit further noticed that in seven divisions® computerized
bills were issued to the consumers from 2011-12 on yearly basis instead of half yearly
basis.

The Chief Engineer, Kashmir, admitted (September/December 2012) that the
computerized data base of consumers was not available with all the Divisions and that
the action required to be taken for computerisation of bills and issuing water charge
bills to the consumers twice a year had been adopted. The Chief Engineer, Jammu
stated (October 2012) that raising of water charge bills twice a year was under
consideration of the Department.

Rule 2.2 of J & K Financial Code stipulate that revenue realized on behalf of the
Government is required to be remitted in full to the nearest treasury on the same or
next working day.

Test-check of records of six divisions” showed that revenue on account of water usage
charges to the extent of € 21.37 lakh collected during the period from March 2007 to
March 2012 had been deposited by the field staff of these divisions into the
Government treasuries after delays ranging between one month and four years'”
resulting in undue retention of Government money with these officials indicating poor
monitoring of revenue receipts. The Chief Engineer, Kashmir stated (December 2012)
that a special team had been framed to conduct Revenue Audit of all the sub-divisions
falling under his jurisdiction. Audit further noticed that against an amount of हैं 0.88
lakh collected between 18 March to 20 March 2012 on account of water usage
charges from the consumers by field staff of Division-I Jammu, only हैं 0.73 lakh had
been deposited (30 March 2012) in the Treasury resulting in short remittance of

4.2.10 Inadequate inspections of water installations

According to Section 22 of J&K Water Supply Act of 1963 and Section 21 of J&K
Water Resources (Regulation and Management Act-2010) the Assistant Engineer or
any Gazetted Officer authorised by the Executive Engineer concerned, may enter into
any premises during day time for the purpose of inspecting any water installation in
any building, site or premises.

Audit noticed that the Department had carried inadequate inspections of water
installations and it was revealed that percentage of inspections of water installations
ranged between 0.03 to 0.19 per cent of the number of connections in two Divisions
(Srinagar and Bijbehara) during the period 2007-08 to 2011-12.

After this was pointed out by audit, the Chief Engineer Kashmir stated (September
2012) that the inspections would be got carried out regularly as per standing rules.
The Chief Engineer Jammu stated (October 2012) that all the Divisions would be
directed to undertake inspections to check the number of irregular connections.

4.2.11 Short levy of penalty for illegal water connections

J &K Water Supply Act, 1963 and Jammu and Kashmir Water Resources (Regulation
and Management) Act, 2010 provide that no person shall, without the authorization or
permission of the Executive Engineer or the prescribed authority, as the case may be,
make or cause to be made, at any time, any connection with the main line in
contravention of the provisions of the Act and whosoever dishonestly takes or makes
any illegal water connection shall be liable, on conviction, to be punished with
imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months and with fine which shall
not be less than one thousand rupees extended to rupees five thousand under the Act of
1963. Under the Act of 2010, a person who had committed such offence is liable on
conviction to be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year
or with fine which may extend to rupees five thousand or with both.

Test-check of records of 12 Divisions revealed that while regularising 30188 illegal
water connections, no penalty was imposed by the Department in respect of 9526
illegal water connections and a meagre penalty ranging between & 200 and & 720 for
each illegal water connection had been imposed by the concerned Executive Engineers
on consumers in respect of 20662 illegal water connections (Kashmir: 5315 Jammu:
15347) during the period 2007-08 to 2011-2012. Against the minimum leviable
penalty of = 3.02 crore in respect of these illegal water connections, penalty of only
& 94.78 lakh was imposed on the defaulters, resulting in short levy of penalty of € 2.07
crore.

stated (September and October 2012) that the amount would be recovered from the

4.2.12 Conclusion

The Performance Audit revealed shortfall in realisation of revenue with reference to
budget estimates of water usage charges and delays in remittance of revenue to the
Government Account. There was no effective system of recovery of revenue from the
consumers which resulted in increase of outstanding revenue during the period 2007-
08 to 2011-12. The regulatory authority under the provisions of the Act, 2010 had
been constituted recently (October 2012). Department had not levied even the
minimum penalty while regularising the illegal water connections.

4.2.13 Recommendations

The Government may consider putting in place:

© a proper system for fixation of targets, framing of Budget estimates on realistic
basis and accurate assessment of revenue on account of water usage charges;
and

° an effective monitoring system to recover the water usage charges, against
various consumers/users of water and the Government money are deposited in
the Government account without any delay.

4.5 Concealment of interstate purchases

Failure of the Assessing Authority to detect concealment of interstate purchases
by the dealer resulted in short levy of tax, interest and penalty of = 7.58 lakh.

The Jammu and Kashmir Value Added Tax Act 2005 (J&K VAT Act) and the Rules
framed thereunder provide that every registered dealer shall submit a quarterly return
containing particulars of sales and purchases together with proof of full payment of
tax due, to the Jurisdictional Assessing Authority within one month from the expiry of
each quarter. Further section 37 of the J &K VAT Act provide that if a registered
dealer has filed the return within the prescribed time and is found to be in order the
return shall be accepted as self assessment by the Assessing Authority.

Audit scrutiny (February 2011) of records of the Commercial Taxes Circle
Srinagar revealed that the dealer had filed quarterly value added tax returns for the
accounting years 2006-07 to 2008-09 which had been accepted as self assessment by
the Assessing Authority, The dealer had concealed the purchases valued at 714.64
lakh’? made by him against issue of ‘C’ forms’ from the dealers located outside the
State. This concealment of purchases received by the dealer could have been detected,
had the assessing authority cross-verified the purchase statements furnished by the
dealer with the accounts of ‘C’ forms issued by the assessing authority for the purpose
of interstate purchase by the dealer. This had resulted in concealment of turnover of
%16.14 lakh” and consequent short levy of tax, interest and penalty of 7.16 lakh’.
